title: Doraemon: Who writes new stories, 30 years after its author died?｜Brand Story
description:
An original manuscript survives, but new stories still need someone to write them. From Mugiwara's recollection of continuing on a separate sheet, we follow Tsujimura and Yakuwa's work on lunar research, friendship, dialogue and the 2019 novelization, then read the 2025 and 2026 credits. The characters are fictional. This production story uses participant interviews and official catalogues; anonymous illustrations are not historical reconstructions.

d1h011.text: Thirty years after its author died, you can still see new Doraemon stories. But if you only notice the “original work” credit,

d1h012.text: you may miss who wrote this version's story.

d1h021.text: Facing the manuscript left behind, assistant Mugiwara was to continue the long-form manga,

d1h022.text: yet he did not draw directly on that sheet.

d1h031.text: I paused here: if he was going to keep drawing, why leave the original untouched?

d1h041.text: Later, another director brought five or six science magazines to a meeting. To send the familiar characters on their way,

d1h042.text: the screenwriter first had to deal with what was already known about the Moon.

d1h051.text: Today, let's follow Doraemon's creative work and see how a sheet of paper passes to the next pair of hands.

d1h061.text: Who actually writes the new stories, and what does the enduring original-work credit do?

d1a011.text: Mugiwara took a fresh sheet of manuscript paper, transferred his mentor's work onto it, then carried on.

d1a012.text: According to his signed message on the memoir's special website, that preserved the original.

d1a021.text: The hovering pen in the opening made me notice a practical choice: you can finish the work in front of you,

d1a022.text: and still leave a place for the original.

d1a023.text: But can that action tell us which installment he took over from?

d1a031.text: The mentor here is Fujiko F. Fujio, whose real surname was Fujimoto.

d1a033.text: Mugiwara later recalled taking over from the third serialized installment of Nobita's Clockwork City Adventure.

d1a041.text: What we found is his later recollection. It cannot establish who drew every page.

d1a051.text: So when you see Doraemon Story from 2017 in a bookshop, is that another year when someone took over?

d1a061.text: Published in August 2017, it is Mugiwara's 130-page memoir manga.

d1a062.text: The publisher says it includes letters and preliminary drawings. That date belongs to the retelling and presentation of those materials.

d1a06b1.text: Why does a catalogue also show 2016 for the same story?

d1a071.text: The Clockwork City Adventure film opened in March 1997, and the collected manga went on sale that August.

d1a072.text: Today's catalogue also lists a 2016 digital release date.

d1a081.text: Separate those dates and the shelf becomes easier to read: a film release, a collected edition and a digital edition

d1a082.text: can each happen at different times.

d1a083.text: A new edition does not move the original creative work to a later year.

d1a091.text: But you may still be waiting for the real difficulty: the old sheet is preserved. When a new adventure is not on that page,

d1a092.text: who decides where the characters go?

d1b011.text: While writing the screenplay for Nobita's Chronicle of the Moon Exploration, released in 2019, Tsujimura received encouragement from Mugiwara.

d1b012.text: In an interview, she said it came in an email.

d1b021.text: She kept asking herself: was she allowed to write dialogue for these characters?

d1b022.text: She recalled the email inviting her to enjoy working on the film and imagine the characters looking forward to another adventure.

d1b031.text: According to Tsujimura, she began to see herself as the person taking everyone on this journey, and could write their dialogue with her head held high.

d1b041.text: I find this interesting: the person who took over the manuscript helped another writer get started.

d1b042.text: Mugiwara also gave limited help with character design on this version and read the final screenplay.

d1b051.text: If you were writing a new adventure for familiar characters, would picking a kingdom no one had heard of be enough to make the story work?

d1b062.text: She wanted viewers leaving the cinema to look up at the Moon and feel it was a little closer than the day before.

d1b071.text: But the Moon was almost too familiar.

d1b072.text: During their discussion, Mugiwara brought out old idea notes. He said he had tried that setting several times before but could not get the story going.

d1b073.text: The more we observe, the less room there is to invent freely.

d1b081.text: Those five or six science magazines in the opening were what director Yakuwa brought to their first discussion.

d1b082.text: Tsujimura recalled discussing the setting with scientific material at that meeting. Even so, writing the screenplay was difficult.

d1b091.text: You see, the research became an obstacle to writing, while also giving the setting boundaries.

d1b092.text: If the Moon were just a blank backdrop for any kingdom, the reason for choosing it would become weaker.

d1b101.text: The writer wanted to set out, and the research was on the table, but the way in was still missing.

d1b102.text: How could the original work's world really connect to this new setting?

d1c011.text: Yakuwa suggested borrowing an existing gadget from an original short manga story to start Nobita's adventure.

d1c012.text: Tsujimura recalled that this suggestion suddenly got the story moving.

d1c02b1.text: But can you simply take an old premise and use it?

d1c02b2.text: If explaining how it works takes too long, the rules may stop viewers before the adventure even begins.

d1c02c1.text: Tsujimura said the original short story had already explained the gadget in a few pages through Nobita's experience,

d1c02c2.text: which made it possible for her to bring it into the film.

d1c02c3.text: Mugiwara also discussed how Fujiko used diagrams to help children follow complex ideas in just a few panels.

d1c02d1.text: So they borrowed more than the name of a premise. They also borrowed a way of making it understandable.

d1c02d2.text: And how should the characters speak?

d1c031.text: Tsujimura also said she could not stand in Fujiko's place and know what he would write. But after years of reading these characters, she could imagine

d1c032.text: what one character would say and what another would do.

d1c041.text: I like that she separates those two things.

d1c051.text: How did the director check whether the adventure's motivation was strong enough?

d1c061.text: Tsujimura said Yakuwa asked her to explain the reason for the adventure and what Luka meant to Nobita.

d1c062.text: Calling him a “friend” was not enough.

d1c071.text: She admitted initially taking it for granted that they would make an effort for a guest character they had just met.

d1c072.text: Those questions made her consider the motivation through Nobita and Luka's particular relationship.

d1c091.text: As you work out those relationships, can a film screenplay keep growing like a novel?

d1d011.text: Tsujimura had to fit dialogue into a limited script length and face the film's running time.

d1d012.text: She said she could decide a novel's length herself, while a film demanded more effective dialogue and a quicker pace.

d1d021.text: If you leave an extra passage in a novel, readers can stop and take their time. In a film,

d1d022.text: those words take up the same stretch of time for every viewer.

d1d023.text: I wonder how she would handle those long speeches.

d1d031.text: She had used long speeches to explain circumstances and feelings. At several points, Yakuwa reminded her that the voice actors' performances and the images

d1d032.text: could convey them, leaving just a shorter line.

d1d061.text: Tsujimura gave another example: the script said only “a mysterious moon.” She did not yet know what color it would be,

d1d062.text: but the animation team could bring that moon into being.

d1d063.text: Once the words are handed over, is the film finished?

d1d071.text: She said the director and crew would continue making the film for about a year and a half after the screenplay was complete.

d1d072.text: So the finished film you see also contains the work of the people who turned those words into images.

d1d081.text: While she was writing the screenplay, Fujiko Pro also invited her to write a novel of the same story.

d1d082.text: She did not agree immediately. She asked: with manga and animation already available, why tell it as a novel too?

d1d091.text: If it merely copied what the film said, you might also ask what the book adds.

d1d092.text: She had to find the work that words themselves could do.

d1d101.text: When the novel's first sentence described the Moon as a harsh world where humans struggle to survive, she realized this was different from a screenplay.

d1d102.text: She could arrange the settings, descriptions and even the way scenes played out herself, through words.

d1d111.text: The colors and sights she could hand over to the animation team now had to return to her pen.

d1d112.text: She described it as making another film herself through a novel, entering the same story from a different angle.

d1d113.text: Would writing it again change her writing speed too?

d1d121.text: She also wrote the characters' feelings at those moments, and scenes absent from the film.

d1d122.text: Tsujimura said she had expected passages with existing images to go faster. Instead, the scenes she had to describe from scratch

d1d123.text: were the ones she wrote more quickly.

d1d12b1.text: And when writing for children, must you make all the vocabulary simpler?

d1d12b2.text: Here, Tsujimura had another choice to make for her readers.

d1d12c1.text: She said she later stopped constantly separating readers by age and hoped both adults and children could read it.

d1d12c2.text: The children's paperback edition adds pronunciation guides to kanji, so she did not deliberately replace lots of them with hiragana. Unfamiliar words

d1d131.text: I think this explains why the same story needs a fresh writer credit: when the medium changes, someone must choose again

d1d132.text: how to make you experience it.

d1d133.text: Does a new novel always wait for the film to open?

d1d141.text: For the 2019 novel, the publisher lists Fujiko F. Fujio for the original work and Tsujimura as the author.

d1d142.text: There is also a separate full-color film comic of the same movie.

d1d14b1.text: The novel went on sale on February 7 that year; the film opened on March 1. The book reached readers before the film.

d1d14b2.text: If you assume every novelization is someone copying a film after its release, this version's dates do not fit.

d1d151.text: And when you pick up the comic-format book, can you immediately assume a manga artist redrew the whole story by hand?

d1e011.text: The full-color Moon Exploration film comic is a comic assembled from the film: an anime film comic.

d1e012.text: The film's completed images can become the contents of such a book. That is different work from drawing a new manga.

d1e021.text: Look instead at the manga version of Nobita's New Dinosaur, and the publisher separates the credits:

d1e022.text: original work by Fujiko F. Fujio, screenplay by Kawamura, manga by Mugiwara.

d1e023.text: That line lays out the work of writing the screenplay and drawing the manga.

d1e031.text: So when you see a familiar name on a shelf, you can look for another field: who wrote it, who drew it,

d1e032.text: or was the film assembled into a book?

d1e033.text: When I read these credits now, I find the version first, then the work.

d1e041.text: Back with recent films, the original-work credit remains. But has the new screenwriter always been the same person?

d1e051.text: For 2025's Nobita's Art World Tales, the production company lists Teramoto as director and Ito as screenwriter.

d1e052.text: The novel of the same name also lists Ito as both author and screenwriter. This version's original work is still credited to Fujiko F. Fujio.

d1e061.text: For 2026's New Nobita and the Undersea Devil's Castle, the official site lists Yajima as director and Murayama as screenwriter.

d1e062.text: The people doing particular jobs change in a new version, while Fujiko remains in the original-work field.

d1e06b1.text: But does a “new screenplay” necessarily mean a story that has never appeared before?

d1e071.text: This one also returns to a 1983 work, adapting a long-form manga into a film again.

d1e072.text: A new screenplay credit can appear on a new adaptation of an old story,

d1e073.text: so the release year alone cannot tell you whether the story is appearing for the first time.

d1e07b1.text: The deluxe disc edition's extras also list a 160-page reduced-size printing of Murayama's screenplay.

d1e07b2.text: A credit can lead you to a specific text, giving interested readers a chance to ask how this version was written.

d1e07c1.text: And can the company names on the official site directly tell you who wrote that screenplay?

d1e081.text: The same 2026 official site also lists the production organizations and Toho as distributor.

d1e082.text: Those fields tell you who participated in production and who handled distribution. To find the writer of this screenplay, read the screenplay field.

d1e091.text: I like that action of taking a fresh sheet of paper.

d1e092.text: Preservation leaves a trail of past work, while those continuing it face today's new problems.

d1e101.text: Doraemon's new stories continue through the creators credited on each version. The original-work credit connects that new work

d1e102.text: back to the world Fujiko F. Fujio created.

d1e111.text: When someone new writes a familiar story, what would you most like to keep? Would you share it in the comments?

d1e121.text: To keep finding the people and work behind familiar names that really move the stories forward, subscribe to this channel.
